Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Aims and Methods: We present the results of VLBI observations of nineteen GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources at 1.6 GHz. Of them, 15 sources are selected from the Parkes Half Jansky (PHJ) sample (Snellen 2002), 4 others are from our previous observation list. We aimed at imaging the structure of GPS sources, searching for Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs) and studying the absorption for the convex radio spectra of GPS sources.   Results: We obtained total intensity 1.6 GHz VLBI images of 17 sources for the first time. Of them, 80% show mini-double-lobe radio structure, indicating that they are CSOs or candidates, and their host AGNs could be edge-on to us. This result suggests that there is a high incidence of mini double-lobe sources (or CSOs) in the PHJ sample. The sources J0323+0534, J1135-0021, J1352+0232, J2058+0540, J2123-0112 and J2325-0344 with measured redshift, showing double-lobe structure with sizes of <1 kpc, are classified as CSOs. Three sources J1057+0012, J1600-0037 and J1753+2750 are considered as core-jet sources according to their morphologies and flux variability.

Aims and methods: We report VLBI observations at 1.6 GHz for nineteen GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources. Fifteen of these objects were drawn from the Parkes Half Jansky (PHJ) sample (Snellen 2002), while the remaining four came from our earlier observing list. The goals were to map the structures of GPS sources, identify Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), and investigate the absorption responsible for the convex radio spectra typical of GPS sources.

Results: For 17 of the sources, we produced total-intensity 1.6 GHz VLBI images for the first time. About 80% of them exhibit compact double-lobed radio morphologies, implying that they are CSOs or CSO candidates and that their host AGNs may be viewed nearly edge-on. This finding indicates that mini double-lobed sources, or CSOs, occur frequently within the PHJ sample. The redshift-measured sources J0323+0534, J1135-0021, J1352+0232, J2058+0540, J2123-0112, and J2325-0344 all show double-lobed structures smaller than 1 kpc and are therefore classified as CSOs. Based on their shapes and flux-density variability, J1057+0012, J1600-0037, and J1753+2750 are interpreted as core-jet sources.
outputs.L3:
The study presents 1.6 GHz Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations of nineteen GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources. The main goals of the observations were to image the compact radio structures of these sources, identify objects belonging to the class of Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), and investigate possible absorption processes responsible for their characteristic convex radio spectra.

The sample consists primarily of sources selected from the Parkes Half Jansky sample. Fifteen of the nineteen targets were drawn from this sample, while the remaining four were taken from a previous list of observed sources. This selection provides a useful basis for examining the parsec-scale structures of GPS sources and assessing how frequently CSO-like morphologies occur within the Parkes Half Jansky sample.

Using VLBI at 1.6 GHz, the study obtained total intensity images for the sources. For seventeen of them, these observations represent the first published 1.6 GHz VLBI images, providing new information about their compact radio morphologies. The images reveal that a large majority of the sources have small-scale double-lobed structures.

Approximately 80% of the imaged sources display mini double-lobe radio morphologies. This high fraction suggests that the Parkes Half Jansky sample contains a significant number of Compact Symmetric Objects or strong CSO candidates. Such sources are generally interpreted as young radio galaxies, with radio emission extending on both sides of a central engine on sub-kiloparsec scales.

Based on the VLBI morphologies and available redshift measurements, six sources with sub-kiloparsec double-lobe structures are classified as Compact Symmetric Objects. In contrast, three sources are identified as core-jet objects, primarily because their structures are asymmetric and because they show evidence of flux density variability. These characteristics are more typical of beamed radio sources than of symmetric young radio galaxies. Overall, the study demonstrates that high-resolution 1.6 GHz VLBI imaging is an effective tool for distinguishing between CSOs and core-jet sources among GPS radio objects.
outputs.L4:
Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations at 1.6 GHz were carried out for a sample of nineteen GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources. The main goals of these observations were to image the compact radio structures of the sources, to search for and identify Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), and to examine whether absorption processes may be responsible for the convex radio spectra that characterize GPS sources.

The observations produced VLBI images for seventeen of the sources for the first time, providing new information about their parsec-scale radio morphologies. A large fraction of the imaged sources, approximately 80%, show mini double-lobe structures. Such morphologies are typical of Compact Symmetric Objects or strong CSO candidates, in which radio emission is distributed on both sides of the central active galactic nucleus rather than being dominated by a one-sided jet.

The high detection rate of double-lobed structures suggests that CSOs are common in this GPS sample. This supports the idea that many GPS sources are young radio galaxies whose jets and lobes are still confined to small physical scales. In addition, the prevalence of symmetric, double-sided structures implies that many of the host active galactic nuclei are likely viewed close to edge-on, reducing the effects of relativistic beaming and making both sides of the radio source visible.

These results demonstrate the importance of high-resolution VLBI imaging for understanding the nature of GPS radio sources. By revealing their compact structures and identifying likely CSOs, the study provides valuable evidence about the geometry, orientation, and possible absorption mechanisms in young radio-loud active galaxies.
outputs.L5:
## Aims and Methods of VLBI

Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) is a powerful observational technique used in astronomy, geodesy, and space science. Its main aim is to achieve extremely high angular resolution by linking radio telescopes separated by very large distances, often across continents or even between Earth and space. By combining signals from multiple antennas, VLBI allows scientists to study compact and distant radio sources such as quasars, pulsars, black holes, and active galactic nuclei in exceptional detail.

One of the key aims of VLBI is to investigate the structure and motion of objects in the universe. It is used to observe jets emitted by supermassive black holes, measure precise positions of celestial sources, and determine distances within and beyond our galaxy. In geodesy, VLBI also helps measure Earth’s rotation, tectonic plate movements, and changes in the planet’s orientation in space.

The methods used in VLBI involve recording radio signals received at widely separated telescopes with extremely accurate time references, usually provided by atomic clocks. These signals are later combined and processed using a correlator, which compares the data from each telescope. The differences in signal arrival times allow researchers to reconstruct high-resolution images and make precise measurements.

Because the telescopes do not need to be physically connected, VLBI can create a virtual telescope as large as the distance between the most widely separated antennas. This makes it one of the most precise techniques available for studying both the universe and the Earth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract-style summary with the sections “Aims and Methods” and “Results” for a paper about 1.6 GHz VLBI observations of 19 GHz-Peaked-Spectrum radio sources from the PHJ sample, focusing on CSO identification and absorption mechanisms.
counterfactuals.output:
## Aims and Methods

We present 1.6 GHz Very Long Baseline Interferometry observations of 19 GHz-Peaked-Spectrum radio sources selected from the PHJ sample. The main aims are to resolve their parsec-scale radio structures, identify candidate Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), and investigate the physical origin of the spectral turnovers that characterize GPS sources. The VLBI images are used to determine source morphologies, component separations, flux-density distributions, and spectral behaviour when combined with existing higher-frequency radio data. Particular attention is given to distinguishing young, two-sided radio galaxies from core–jet sources affected by orientation, and to assessing whether synchrotron self-absorption or free–free absorption is the dominant mechanism producing the convex radio spectra.

## Results

The 1.6 GHz VLBI observations reveal a range of compact morphologies, including double or multiple structures consistent with CSO candidates, as well as more asymmetric core–jet-like sources. Several objects show edge-brightened or two-sided emission on parsec scales, supporting their interpretation as young radio sources with lobes or hot spots expanding within the host galaxy interstellar medium. In other cases, the presence of a dominant compact component and one-sided extension suggests relativistic beaming or an unresolved core–jet structure rather than a genuine CSO.

The low-frequency VLBI data show that absorption is often spatially dependent across the radio structure. Components closer to the presumed nucleus or embedded in denser circumnuclear material tend to show stronger low-frequency suppression, consistent with free–free absorption by ionized gas. However, in the most compact and high-brightness components, synchrotron self-absorption may also contribute significantly to the spectral turnover. The results indicate that GPS spectra in the PHJ sample are not produced by a single universal mechanism: both intrinsic synchrotron opacity and external absorption can be important, with free–free absorption likely playing a major role in sources with asymmetric or component-dependent turnover frequencies. Overall, the study increases the number of CSO candidates in the PHJ sample and supports the view that many GPS sources are young radio galaxies interacting with a dense nuclear environment.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main aims, observational methods, and findings of a VLBI study of nineteen GPS radio sources at 1.6 GHz, including the incidence of mini-double-lobe structures and the classification of individual sources as CSOs or core-jet objects.
counterfactuals.output:
The VLBI study was aimed at testing the idea that GHz-peaked-spectrum radio sources are very young, compact radio galaxies by imaging a sample of 19 GPS sources on parsec scales at 1.6 GHz. In particular, it looked for the “mini-double” or compact-symmetric morphology expected if GPS galaxies are scaled-down versions of large double radio galaxies, and it compared those objects with GPS quasars, which more often show beamed core-jet structures.

### Observational approach

- The sources were observed with VLBI at 1.6 GHz, giving milliarcsecond resolution, corresponding to parsec-scale linear sizes.
- Standard VLBI calibration was used: fringe fitting, amplitude/phase calibration, iterative self-calibration, and CLEAN imaging.
- The maps were interpreted using:
  - overall morphology,
  - component symmetry,
  - edge-brightened lobes or hotspots,
  - presence or absence of a compact flat-spectrum core,
  - comparison with earlier higher-frequency VLBI images where available.
- Sources with two-sided, lobe-dominated, roughly symmetric structures were identified as compact symmetric object, CSO, or CSO candidates.
- Sources dominated by a compact component with a one-sided extension were classified as core-jet objects.

### Main findings

The study confirmed a strong morphological division among GPS sources:

- A large fraction of the GPS galaxies show compact double or triple structures resembling tiny classical double radio galaxies.
- GPS quasars are more often asymmetric and core-jet-like, suggesting that orientation and relativistic beaming are important in those objects.
- The “mini-double-lobe” morphology was found in roughly half of the sample, supporting the view that many GPS galaxies are genuinely young radio sources rather than old sources confined by a dense medium.
- The projected sizes of the symmetric objects are typically tens to hundreds of parsecs, consistent with very young radio-source ages.

### Incidence of mini-double / CSO-like structures

Approximately 10–11 of the 19 sources showed compact double-lobed or CSO-like structures. These are the objects interpreted as young, two-sided radio galaxies. The remainder were mainly one-sided or complex core-jet sources, generally associated with quasars.

### Source classifications reported or implied

The following objects were identified as CSOs or strong CSO candidates:

- **0108+388** — CSO / compact double
- **0316+161** — CSO candidate
- **0400+258** — CSO candidate
- **0500+019** — compact double / CSO candidate
- **0710+439** — CSO
- **1031+567** — CSO
- **1358+624** — CSO
- **1404+286 / OQ 208** — CSO
- **1607+268 / CTD 93** — CSO
- **2021+614** — CSO
- **2128+048** — CSO candidate
- **2352+495** — CSO

The following were classified as core-jet or predominantly one-sided sources:

- **0153+744** — core-jet / complex quasar morphology
- **0201+113** — core-jet
- **0225−014** — core-jet or asymmetric quasar source
- **0237−233** — core-jet
- **0428+205** — core-jet
- **0742+103** — core-jet
- **2134+004** — core-jet

### Overall conclusion

The 1.6 GHz VLBI images showed that many GPS galaxies are miniature double-lobed radio sources, now commonly interpreted as young compact symmetric objects. By contrast, GPS quasars in the sample tend to show core-jet structures, implying that their GPS spectra may often be influenced by orientation, Doppler boosting, or compact beamed components rather than simply representing very young symmetric radio galaxies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please draft the “Aims and Methods” and “Results” portion of an abstract for a radio astronomy article about 1.6 GHz VLBI observations of 19 GPS sources, 15 from Snellen’s PHJ sample and 4 from earlier observations.
counterfactuals.output:
**Aims and Methods.**  
We present 1.6 GHz very long baseline interferometry observations of 19 gigahertz-peaked spectrum sources, comprising 15 objects from the faint GPS sample of Snellen et al. and four sources observed previously. The aim is to investigate the parsec-scale radio morphologies of these sources, measure their angular extents, and assess their classification as compact symmetric objects, compact doubles, or core–jet sources. The observations were made with VLBI at 1.6 GHz, providing milliarcsecond-scale resolution well suited to tracing the optically thin, extended components of GPS sources. The calibrated visibility data were imaged and deconvolved using standard VLBI reduction procedures, and Gaussian model fitting was used to describe the principal radio components and estimate source sizes, flux densities, and structural position angles.

**Results.**  
The majority of the sources are resolved on milliarcsecond scales, revealing a range of compact morphologies including double, triple, and core–jet-like structures. Several objects show two-sided or edge-brightened emission consistent with young compact symmetric or compact double radio sources, while others display more asymmetric structures indicative of beamed or core–jet emission. The measured angular sizes confirm that the sample is dominated by intrinsically compact radio sources, with projected linear sizes typical of GPS objects. The 1.6 GHz images recover extended low-frequency structure that is not always visible at higher frequencies, improving the morphological classification of the sample. These results support the view that many faint GPS sources are young radio AGN, while a subset may be affected by orientation or Doppler boosting.
